title: BASIC DAIRY NUTRITION
text:
BASIC DAIRY NUTRITION

Objectives:
1. To know the importance of good nutrition in dairy cattle.
2. To learn the basic feed nutrients.

Importance of improved nutrition in dairy animals:
1. for breeding efficiency and reproduction
- A well-nourished cattle increases libido in bulls and improves fertility of heifers and cows. Good nutrition also speeds up the recovery of the uterus after calving.
2. for body maintenance
- Nutrient requirements of animals are different and it is primarily impacted by weight, age, breed, physiological status, activity and environment.

Age (Months) | 3 | 6 | 9 | 15 | 20
% Mature Weight | 20% | 30% | 40% | 60% | 90%
Mature Weight (kg) | Target weight (kg) at different ages
450 (Jersey) | 90 | 135 | 180 | 270 | 405
500 (Holstein x Jersey) | 100 | 150 | 200 | 300 | 450
550 (Holstein) | 110 | 165 | 220 | 330 | 495

3. for higher milk yield.
- High producing dairy cow requires a diet that supplies the nutrient needs for high milk production.

Category / Lactation period | Milk yield (L/day) | CP req | MjME/KgDM | First limiting factor | Best Feed
Early lactation | 15-22 | 18% | 11.0 | Protein | Forage plus high protein concentrate
Mid lactation | 12-15 | 16% | 10.8 | Protein & Energy | Forage plus high protein concentrate
Late lactation | 8-12 | 14% | 10.6 | Energy & Protein | Forage/Roughage plus low volume of concentrate
Dry cow 12% | 0 | 12% | 10.4 | Energy | Forage/Roughage
Young Stock | 0 | 16-18% | 11.0 | Protein & Energy | Pasture/Forage plus high protein concentrate

facts: The learning objectives of the section are to know the importance of good nutrition in dairy cattle and to learn the basic feed nutrients.
Improved nutrition is important for breeding efficiency and reproduction: it increases libido in bulls, improves fertility in heifers and cows, and speeds up uterine recovery after calving.
Nutrient requirements for body maintenance are primarily impacted by weight, age, breed, physiological status, activity, and environment.
At 3 months of age, cattle target weight is 20% of mature weight (90 kg for Jersey, 100 kg for Holstein x Jersey, 110 kg for Holstein).
At 6 months of age, cattle target weight is 30% of mature weight (135 kg for Jersey, 150 kg for Holstein x Jersey, 165 kg for Holstein).
At 9 months of age, cattle target weight is 40% of mature weight (180 kg for Jersey, 200 kg for Holstein x Jersey, 220 kg for Holstein).
At 15 months of age, cattle target weight is 60% of mature weight (270 kg for Jersey, 300 kg for Holstein x Jersey, 330 kg for Holstein).
At 20 months of age, cattle target weight is 90% of mature weight (405 kg for Jersey, 450 kg for Holstein x Jersey, 495 kg for Holstein).
Assumed mature weights are 450 kg for Jersey, 500 kg for Holstein x Jersey cross, and 550 kg for Holstein.
Improved nutrition is essential for higher milk yield because high-producing cows require diets supplying specific high-yield nutrient needs.

During early lactation, milk yield is 15-22 L/day, crude protein requirement is 18%, energy density is 11.0 MjME/KgDM, the first limiting factor is protein, and the best feed is forage plus high protein concentrate.

During mid lactation, milk yield is 12-15 L/day, crude protein requirement is 16%, energy density is 10.8 MjME/KgDM, the first limiting factors are protein & energy, and the best feed is forage plus high protein concentrate.

During late lactation, milk yield is 8-12 L/day, crude protein requirement is 14%, energy density is 10.6 MjME/KgDM, the first limiting factors are energy & protein, and the best feed is forage/roughage plus low volume of concentrate.
For a dry cow, milk yield is 0 L/day, crude protein requirement is 12%, energy density is 10.4 MjME/KgDM, the first limiting factor is energy, and the best feed is forage/roughage.

For young stock, milk yield is 0 L/day, crude protein requirement is 16-18%, energy density is 11.0 MjME/KgDM, the first limiting factors are protein & energy, and the best feed is pasture/forage plus high protein concentrate.
